seed.relationship: a new teacher and a wary student
seed.topicSeed: a hillside terrace in Naples; a new teacher and a wary student over who should stay behind

g.passage: Who decides which child stays behind when the olives must be carried down? So the old tellers on the terraces above Naples begin this tale. A young teacher named Emilio came to the hill school and announced that the slowest reader would stay to tend the trees while the others went to market. Alessia, who read slowly but counted quickly, folded her arms and said nothing. On market day Emilio found the baskets tallied wrong and the prices muddled, for no one else could reckon so well, and he climbed back up the hill red-faced to fetch her. The tellers say he never again chose by a single measure, though they add, with a wink, that he took a long time to admit it aloud. Even now, grandmothers who repeat the story pause here to slice bread, and the children wait, chins on hands, for the ending they already know.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Emilio?
options: Openly scornful, presenting him as a fool who never learns from his error
Deeply admiring, presenting his choice as wise from the very beginning
Gently amused, treating his mistake as forgivable while noting his pride
Coolly detached, reporting his actions without any hint of judgment

seed.relationship: a landlord's son and a tenant's daughter
seed.conflict: while learning to let go of a habit

g.passage: Three clothespins per shirt, two per towel, one per sock: Ximena had hung her family's laundry by these rules on the Cairo rooftop since she was eight. Tariq, the landlord's son, liked to watch her count them out from the stairwell. One afternoon the wind came hard off the desert, and he ran up to help, pinning sheets any way he could, sometimes with four pins, sometimes with none. Ximena nearly scolded him. Instead she watched the sheets snap and hold, and she noticed that not one had fallen. The next week she left a few towels hanging by a single pin, just to see. They dried as quickly as the others. Below the roof, a vendor called out the price of guavas, and pigeons settled in a row along the water tank.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A girl begins to loosen a strict routine after seeing it was less necessary than she believed.
A girl and a boy work together to keep the family laundry from blowing off a windy roof.

Helping one's neighbors during difficult weather is the best way to build a friendship.

g.passage: Four trays of dough, two ovens, one hour before the doors open: that was the rule of the bakery in Kerala where Camille and I worked the summer after the storm. We had not spoken properly in years, Camille and I, though we kneaded at the same table. Kenji, the owner, assumed we were simply quiet people. Then the flood washed out the garden behind the shop and uncovered a tin box our grandmother had buried there, full of letters she had written to each of us and never sent. Camille read hers standing in the mud. I read mine by the ovens. Neither of us said what was inside. But the next morning she slid the sugar jar toward me before I asked for it, and I held the oven door for her tray. Kenji, noticing nothing, complained about the price of cardamom.

g.passage: Chalk dust and the smell of the harbor still drift through this classroom in Marseille, Remy, and I am writing to you from my desk during the break. You will laugh, but I am learning French verbs at seventy so that I can finally read the street signs I have walked past my whole life. When Theo first came to my fish stall, he was lost and could not read them either. I drew him a map on a scrap of wrapping paper, with a fish where my stall was and a star for his school. He still carries it, though he knows the way now. Last week he copied the street names for me into a notebook, slowly, letter by letter, and quizzed me as I sorted the mackerel. Tell your mother the boats came in late this morning, and the gulls were louder than the teacher.

To explain why the writer decided to sell fish near a language school in Marseille
To describe the route that Theo once followed from the fish stall to his school

g.passage: "You going to finish that boat, or just sit with it?" Devon called from the end of the dock. Amelie did not answer. The half-built skiff had rested on two sawhorses beside the lake for nine summers, ever since she and Devon had begun it together and then quarreled over the shape of the bow. Neither had touched it since, though both still walked past it most evenings. This evening Amelie had brought a plane and a jar of nails. She ran her hand along the bow, the curve Devon had wanted, and did not reshape it. When he came closer, she held out a second hammer, handle first, and waited. Out on the water, a heron lifted from the reeds and flew low toward the cypress trees.
g.question: Based on the passage, why does Amelie most likely hold out a second hammer to Devon?
options: She hopes to resume the shared project and mend the old quarrel with him.
She wants to prove that the boat's bow was built correctly from the start.
She is irritated by his remark and wants him to do the hardest work himself.
She needs the boat finished quickly before the lake's summer season ends.

g.passage: Two buses an hour climbed past the stop on the ridge road outside Lagos, and Sergio had already let three of them go. The letter in his pocket offered him a place on a club in another city, where he would start every match instead of watching from the bench. Nneka, his coach, sat beside him on the concrete bench, saying nothing about it. She had benched him all season for missing practices, and he had called her unfair in front of the team. Yet that morning she had written to the other club herself, praising his speed and his footwork. Sergio had seen the copy on her desk. When the fourth bus came, he stood, shook her hand for a long moment, and boarded. Nneka watched it disappear around the bend, then walked back down to sweep the training field.
g.question: Based on the passage, why does Sergio most likely shake Nneka's hand for a long moment before boarding?
options: He wants to show her that he has forgiven her for keeping him on the bench all season.
He has realized she helped him get the offer, and he wishes to thank her for it.

g.passage: When I was twelve, I broke my father's bicycle chain on a Dhaka curb and carried the pieces to Hari's shoe repair stall, because Hari could mend anything with leather and wire. I had already rehearsed a story about a careless rickshaw driver. Hari listened, nodding, then asked me to hold the chain while he worked. As he threaded each link, he told me how, as a boy, he had blamed a stray dog for a torn sandal and how his own father had believed him for thirty years. "He still mentions that dog," Hari said. "I have never had the courage to correct him." That evening I told my father the chain broke because I had jumped the curb too fast. He sighed, and then he laughed. Outside our window the street vendors were packing up their carts of mangoes for the night.
g.question: Based on the passage, why does Putri most likely tell her father the truth about the chain?
options: She fears that Hari will report the accident to her father if she does not.
She wants her father to laugh with her about how foolishly she had ridden.
She is upset that the rickshaw driver would be blamed and punished unfairly.
Hari's story shows her the lasting weight of a lie that is never corrected.

g.passage: Oaxaca was dry that March, and the river we crossed to reach my grandmother's village was only stones and cracked mud. Halfway across, Esperanza stopped and asked me to say my full name aloud. I said Eulalio, the name on my school papers, the name everyone used. She shook her head and told me the other one, the name of her own brother, which my parents had written second on my birth record and then forgotten. He had drowned in this same river, she said, in a year when it ran high. Then she made me repeat his name three times, standing on the stones where the water used to be, until she was satisfied that I would not lose it. I did not understand her then. At the far bank, a boy was selling cold tamarind drinks from a cooler, and we each bought one.
g.question: Based on the passage, why does Esperanza most likely make Eulalio repeat the second name?
options: She wants the memory of her drowned brother to be carried on by her grandson.
She is annoyed that Eulalio uses only the name written on his school papers.
She believes saying the name will protect the boy from the river's floodwaters.
She plans to have the boy's school records changed to show his second name.

g.passage: "Translate only what I say, nothing more," Somchai told me the first day, and so I have, Mother, for six weeks in this printing room in Chiang Mai. Yesterday the investors asked him who had designed the new type press. Somchai looked at the young mechanic oiling the rollers, then said the design was his own. I knew otherwise; I had seen the mechanic's drawings pinned above his bench. Later Somchai explained, quietly, that the mechanic's family owes money to the very men who were asking, and that a name on a patent would bring them knocking. I translated his claim exactly as he spoke it. I said nothing about the drawings, though my face burned. This morning the presses are running early, and the whole room smells of ink and wet paper. Please send the recipe for the mango rice.

g.passage: Isadora had sold her pies at the roadside diner outside Porto Alegre for twenty years, and the spring her daughter Maya was to marry, a travel magazine named them the best on the southern highway. Customers lined up before dawn. Isadora baked through the nights and still could not keep up, and the wedding plans lay untouched beneath a sack of flour. One evening she hung a sign on the door: closed for ten days, family matters. Regulars grumbled; a reporter called twice. Maya found her mother at the kitchen table with the guest list, which she had not looked at in weeks. Isadora remembered aloud how her own mother had missed her wedding to cover a shift, and how the empty chair still seemed to stand in every photograph. The folktale tellers say the pies tasted better when the diner reopened, though the recipe never changed.

g.passage: Ayesha did not trust her new hire. Lanying had joined the galley crew at the Karachi docks only a week earlier, and already she had reorganized the spice shelves and asked why the cooks worked double shifts while the officers' steward worked none. Ayesha had worked those double shifts for eleven years. She had missed her son's school prizes and her mother's last birthday for them. Now, chopping onions beside the girl, she felt the old resentment stir, and beneath it something less familiar, a small flicker of hope that someone might finally say aloud what she had swallowed. She caught herself watching Lanying's quick hands with something close to pride. Still she said only, "Mind the knife," and pushed the cutting board an inch farther away. The ship's engine shuddered beneath them, and the pots swung on their hooks.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?

g.passage: Bamboo ribs lay drying in rows across the kite-maker's yard in Hanoi when Chinedu, the mayor, came to say the clinic would close. The town could not pay for it, he told Budi, its only doctor, and he had signed the order that morning. Budi said nothing at first. He picked up a half-finished kite and tested its frame, as he did when patients told him bad news. Chinedu went on listing reasons, more of them than were needed, and his voice grew softer with each one. Twice he glanced at the children chasing a red kite above the wall, the same children Budi had treated for fever in the rainy season. At last he folded the order into his pocket rather than handing it over, and asked how much paper a kite like that would need. Overhead, the red kite dipped, caught a gust, and climbed.

Tense and somber, gradually giving way to a quiet, uncertain hope
Hopeful and confident, with a slight undercurrent of tension
Bitter and accusatory, reflecting the doctor's anger at the mayor

g.passage:
By four o'clock the kiln had cooled enough to open,
and Hollis stood with her hand on its iron door
while Grant, the delivery boy, argued about the boxes:
ten, he said, not twelve; the invoice was wrong.
She argued back as if the count could matter,
as if the clay her husband wedged each spring
were not still drying, unfinished, on his shelf.
Grant raised his voice; she raised hers higher.
Between them, frost was gathering on the window,
and the bowls inside the kiln, still warm,
held the last glaze he had mixed, a blue
she had not dared to open all winter.
When Grant fell silent, she pulled the door.
Steam rose. One bowl had cracked along the rim.
The others shone. She counted them aloud,
softly, twice, and signed for ten.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the poem?
options: Irritable and combative, with grief appearing only in a single brief image
Calm and accepting, as the speaker finally makes peace with a quiet loss
Grief-laden beneath a surface of petty irritation that slowly gives way
Nostalgic and fond, focused on happy memories of a shared craft
g.explanation: 시는 상자 개수를 두고 다투는 짜증 섞인 표면 아래에, 선반 위에서 마르고 있는 남편의 미완성 점토와 겨우내 열지 못한 그의 마지막 유약이라는 슬픔의 단서를 여러 곳에 둔다. 다툼이 잦아들고 그녀가 부드럽게 그릇을 세며 열 개에 서명하는 장면까지 이으면 슬픔이 더 두드러진 어조이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 두 정서의 비중을 뒤집었고, B는 끝부분의 차분함만 본 덜 두드러진 정서다. D는 도예라는 소재와 어울리지만 행복한 추억의 단서가 약하다.
